_comment: C0-5 body translation for coding/openai-dot. The source quotes official wording in Chinese translation; per B-class rules the English side renders those quotes back in English marked (translated) — no fabricated originals. Keys align with build.mjs.
_rules: 0) Keep ** emphasis, `code`, links and table structure, block-for-block with the Chinese side.
1) Official English quotes stay verbatim; Chinese-rendered paraphrases of official wording are marked (translated) on the English side — never fabricate English originals.
2) Do not upgrade 'unverified / not stated officially' semantics; the translation changes no facts.

axes.model_access:
**The model is not user-selectable; it is vendor-assigned** —

**official launch-page wording**: "powered by GPT-6 Astra" (translated).

i.e.: Dot runs on GPT-6 Astra, with no model-selection entry point.

This contrasts with the IDE / CLI forms in this section: there the model is usually selectable,
while **the vendor-cloud form takes the whole "pick a model" decision away**.
axes.runtime:
**The answer to "what form is it" is the product itself**:

**official wording**: "a separate computer in the cloud" (translated), with "its own browser" (translated),
and "you can open the Dot's computer at any time to check its work" (translated).

The official pages also state another authorization mode: "you can also authorize Dot to connect to and use your own devices,
e.g. a laptop, so it collaborates with you directly in your working environment" (translated) —

**so runtime has two modes**: the vendor cloud VM by default, with optional authorized access to your own machine.
axes.local_files:
**Fully isolated by default**. Official wording (translated):
"unless you choose to connect your own computer, your computer and its contents always remain isolated from it".
Dot's files all live in its own cloud environment.

**What it can do once authorized to connect locally — the official security document gives concrete examples** (supplemented 2026-10-03, translated):
"you can also choose to connect your own computer so Dot can help in more ways,
e.g. **analyzing a spreadsheet saved on your desktop**, or using programming tools installed on the device".

So local authorization is not one "file access" toggle;
it covers **desktop files + development tools installed on the device**.

**Inside the cloud workspace there is another sandbox layer** (translated):
"within each Dot's protected workspace, **sandboxing limits the code and tools that Dot can access**,
helping contain the blast radius of harmful code or mistaken commands".

**Multi-tenant isolation is also stated** (translated): "isolating different users' cloud environments from each other",
and "the environment where Dot runs code is **separate from** the systems that coordinate its work and **enforce key safeguards**".

**⚠ How far read-only tools can actually read inside connected apps still has no quantified official boundary**
(only negative descriptions like "cannot send messages or change app content").
axes.background:
**This dimension is its strongest one; the official pages devote a whole section** (translated):
"even when you are not directly interacting with a Dot, it looks in the background for ways to help.
We call this 'proactive research'."

The official pages also state work keeps progressing after you close the app,
and **"your Dot can pick up a project and drive it forward autonomously, even while it is juggling several others at the same time"** (translated).
**Multi-task parallelism is an officially stated capability, not speculation**.

**Workspaces are persistent** (translated): "each Dot has its own cloud computer where it can browse the web,
analyze information, create files and run tools. Even when you are not actively involved,
Dots can **keep work moving forward** in these workspaces".

⚠ **During "proactive research" it uses read-only tools** — official wording (translated):
"in doing so it accesses your connected apps through tools with read-only permissions.
These tools cannot send messages, change app content, or control your browser or computer".

**This qualifier matters**: background autonomy ≠ background write access.
**⚠ Background work does not run unconditionally** (supplemented 2026-10-03):
the official security document states monitoring can pause it mid-execution —

"if safety monitoring detects risk in work a Dot is doing, **it can pause that work**
and show you a warning" (translated); the launch-page version says "can pause or stop a Dot's work" (translated).
**So the accurate statement of "keeps going after shutdown" is: keeps going, but may be intercepted mid-way.**
axes.tools:
**The plugin ecosystem is the core selling point**; official wording (translated): "through our plugin ecosystem,
they can easily connect to more than 4,000 apps".

The official pages state the app source is "apps you have connected",
with built-in app controls to manage permissions.

Also: coding tasks can be handed to Codex (at DevDay, Codex itself was also announced going cloud);
working with Microsoft to bring dedicated Dots into Agent 365 governance and security controls.
axes.context:
**Context persists across channels** — official wording (translated):
"dots keep context across channels, so whichever channel you reach them through,
they have the full picture".

Channels include:

- ChatGPT (desktop/web/mobile)
- Slack
- Teams
- SMS (officially "coming soon")
- Voice calls

**The carrier of cross-channel sharing is stated officially as "projects"** (translated):
"you can start a project in ChatGPT, **share context with the team on that project via Slack**,
and let the dot keep the work moving" —

i.e. context hangs on the project rather than on a channel, which is the mechanistic precondition for going cross-channel.

The official pages stress the learning mechanism: "learns from feedback over long use"; "the more you work together,
the more Dot understands your preferences, how you think, and what you consider good work" (translated).

**⚠ Training data is not used to improve models by default, but there is one important exception** (supplemented 2026-10-03,
previously missed in this dossier): official wording (translated) "by default, we **do not** use content from
ChatGPT Business, Enterprise or Edu workspaces to improve our models".

**The statement is scoped to three workspace tiers** — per the launch page wording,
for personal and Pro tiers this page gives **no equivalent statement**, and whether the tiers differ is not explained on the official pages. **Do not generalize "not used for training" to all tiers.**

**Context-window size and memory storage implementation — neither official page gives numbers.**
axes.permissions:
**This dossier has the most complete permission information of the three; the official pages have two dedicated sections.**

Three layers:

① Custom rules — **official wording** (translated): "with custom rules you can allow specific actions,
require approval first, or block them", and **"built-in safety requirements always apply"**
(i.e. custom rules can only tighten above the official floor, never loosen it);

② Automated review — **"for actions that could affect your account or share information, Dot runs automated review"** (translated),
the official criteria being "whether it matches your instructions, custom rules and safety requirements",
and it explicitly states "certain sensitive tasks like changing passwords always require you personally" (translated);

③ Credential isolation — "when logging into supported sites, Dot can use saved passwords
without revealing them to the model" (translated).

**④ Runtime monitoring really does intervene (supplemented 2026-10-03; this layer was previously missing)**:
the official security document states (translated) "we also **monitor Dot as it plans and executes actions**,
looking for potentially harmful behavior, e.g. going beyond your instructions or attempting to bypass safeguards.

**If safety monitoring detects risk in work a Dot is doing, it can pause that work
and show you a warning for you to review**".

**This is evidence of "review" and "execution" being separated** — it does not only gate before actions;
it can also stop mid-execution.

This is the layer closest to Meta Muse's "approval handed to another agent",
but the official pages **never state whether this monitor is independent of the model** (Muse explicitly states Sentinel system-level isolation;
Dot does not) — **do not fill this in for them.**

**Audit surface**: the official pages provide an activity view to follow progress including background work.

⚠ The same official page also states **"Dots can still make mistakes, so be sure to check work products that could have significant consequences"** (translated).
axes.fit:
What the official pages give are **role-based scenarios**, worth copying directly as a selection basis (translated):

- turning feedback into tested fixes (delivering a full PR with a demo video)
- adjusting release plans when product scope changes
- re-running analyses and updating paper figures when new evidence arrives
- keeping sales proposals updated as requirements change
- content production running automatically

Conversely it **does not fit**: people who want to pick their own model; people whose data cannot leave the machine;
people needing fine-grained control with takeover at any moment (local IDE/CLI forms fit better).

sectionTitles.与本分区另两组形态的根本差别: The fundamental difference from the other two form groups in this section
sectionTitles.后台自主 ≠ 后台可改（这一条最容易被误读）: Background autonomy ≠ background write access (the easiest point to misread)
sectionTitles.权限：三层，其中一层是官方底线: Permissions: three layers, one of which is the official floor
sectionTitles.凭据：不向模型暴露密码: Credentials: passwords never exposed to the model
sectionTitles.计费：一句话，但有个坑: Billing: one sentence, but with a trap
sectionTitles.安全文档给出的三条硬机制（此前档案缺这一整块）: Three hard mechanisms from the security document (this whole block was previously missing)

sections.与本分区另两组形态的根本差别:
This is not "yet another AI coding tool" but **a different direction**:

| | IDE form / CLI form | Vendor-cloud form (this entry) |
|---|---|---|
| Installed where | your machine | the vendor's cloud VM |
| Who picks the model | usually selectable | **vendor-assigned** (GPT-6 Astra) |
| After shutdown | stops | **keeps running** |
| Local files | direct read/write | **isolated by default**; connecting locally needs explicit authorization |
| Approval | confirmed case by case in the chat/terminal | custom rules + automated review + sensitive actions always human |

**So its irreplaceable point is not "more features" but "it works even when your machine is offline".**
sections.后台自主 ≠ 后台可改（这一条最容易被误读）:
The official pages devote a whole section to background behavior, worth quoting in full
(the source quotes it as a Chinese translation of the official English; rendered back with the (translated) marker):

```
Even when you are not directly interacting with a Dot, it looks in the background
for ways to help. We call this "proactive research". In doing so, it accesses your
connected apps through tools with read-only permissions. That means these tools
cannot send messages, change app content, or control your browser or computer.
(translated)
```

**The qualifier is stated clearly**: background autonomous actions get **read-only** tools.

**Put differently**: "it works on its own while I am away" holds; "it sends messages or changes content on my behalf while I am away" does not.
If this site previously understood it as the latter, that was reading past the official one-line qualifier.
sections.权限：三层，其中一层是官方底线:
The official pages split permissions into three explicit blocks, which is useful for selection (compare layer by layer, no guessing):

| Layer | Key official wording (translated) | How tight can you set it |
|---|---|---|
| Custom rules | "you can allow specific actions, require approval first, or block them" | entirely yours |
| Built-in safety requirements | "built-in safety requirements always apply" | **the floor; your rules can only tighten above it** |
| Automated review | "automated review checks whether it matches your instructions, custom rules and safety requirements" | criteria include all three above |

Plus one hard boundary:

```
Certain sensitive tasks like changing passwords always require you personally. (translated)
```

**"Custom rules can only tighten above the official floor, never loosen it" is the most valuable information in this layer** —
it means when configuring rules you need not worry about setting them too loose; the vendor has a backstop.
sections.凭据：不向模型暴露密码:
```
When logging into supported sites, Dot can use saved passwords
without revealing them to the model. (translated)
```

This is the same design family as Meta Muse's Secure Credentials Store:
**credentials go to a "vault"; the model only gets "permission to finish this task with the credentials"**.
Both vendors independently adopted this pattern, worth noting —
vendor consensus on agent credentials is converging.
sections.计费：一句话，但有个坑:
```
Your first Dot is included with Pro or Business Premium plans, at no extra cost. (translated)
```

**But** the same page has two easy-to-miss qualifiers:

| Scenario | Counted against ChatGPT usage quota? |
|---|---|
| Chats with the Dot itself | **not counted** (official wording translated: "conversations with Dot do not use your ChatGPT usage limits") |
| Tasks a Dot starts or manages inside Codex / ChatGPT work | **counted as usual** |

i.e.: **chatting with your Dot is free, but the work it dispatches on your behalf is billed as usual.**

Also, Enterprise (incl. Edu / Healthcare) is off by default; workspace admins must enable the beta.

| Page | Status |

| Introducing Dot launch page | ✅ Playwright rendered capture of 5,166 words; all eight dimensions evidenced from the body |
| DevDay 2026 recap | ✅ captured (Dots plan scope, Enterprise beta off by default) |

| Dot security document · how-we-build-safety | ✅ **full page body captured 2026-10-03**, filling the `local_files` / `background` / `permissions` dimensions |

**⚠ Confidence remains partial, but the gaps have narrowed to two classes**:
before the supplement it was "the security document was never read";
now the implementation path of the safety mechanisms is in hand (sandbox / isolation / runtime monitoring / execution-environment separation),

and what remains genuinely absent from the official pages is:
① **quantified metrics** (detection rate and false-positive rate of the monitoring system, read boundaries of read-only tools);
② **context-window size and memory storage implementation**.

Two more "the official pages do not say whether this is the case" items must stay unknown:
whether the runtime monitor is **independent of the model**, and whether the "content not used to improve models" statement **covers the personal and Pro tiers**.
sections.安全文档给出的三条硬机制（此前档案缺这一整块）:
The biggest gain of this supplemental verification was finding the security document itself. It gives three **checkable mechanisms**:

| Mechanism | Key official wording (translated) |
|---|---|
| **Workspace sandbox** | "sandboxing limits the code and tools that Dot can access, helping contain the blast radius of harmful code or mistaken commands" |
| **Multi-tenant isolation** | "isolating different users' cloud environments from each other" |
| **Execution separated from safeguards** | "the environment where Dot runs code is **separate from** the systems that coordinate its work and enforce key safeguards" |

The third is the **same design orientation** as Meta Muse's Sentinel —
both vendors place key safeguards outside the model. This is not coincidence; it is a shared convergence point of vendor-cloud agents.

**The official pages also acknowledge prompt injection and its mitigations** (translated):
"webpages, emails or documents may contain malicious instructions attempting to redirect the agent's actions
or trick it into sharing private information — a problem called **prompt injection**.
We combine model-level protections with **tool restrictions, pre-action checks and monitoring**".

**Note this document also holds back**: "human and automated red-teaming help us find weaknesses,
improve the model and the systems around it, and **test those improvements again**" —
no detection-rate numbers are given anywhere, so gap ① above is **genuinely undisclosed by the vendor**, not something this site failed to find.

runs:
This site has not completed measured runs. The test protocol is at [protocols/coding/_protocol.md](../../../protocols/coding/_protocol.md).

**Suggested measurement**: the comparison dimensions of these three vendor-cloud agents concentrate in `background` and `permissions`;
they cannot be installed locally (requires a Pro / Business Premium subscription),

**so measurement must rely on external observation like "is it still moving after I close the client"**,
not local benchmarks.

- Form factor and quota accounting are verified; no need to re-test.
unknowns:
- Context-window size and the concrete implementation of memory
- Trigger conditions and frequency of "proactive research"
- How far connected apps can actually be read under **read-only** tools (official pages give only negative descriptions)
- Detection rate / false-positive rate of the safety monitoring system (official pages only mention "red-teaming", no numbers)
- Whether the runtime monitor is independent of the model (Muse states Sentinel isolation; Dot does not state)
- Whether "customer content is not used to improve models" also covers the personal and Pro tiers (official pages only name Business/Enterprise/Edu)
- Rollout differences by region/account
